metadata.title: Snow Queen is Evil and Beautiful: Experimental Evidence for Probabilistic Contextuality in Human Choices

extraction_notes.note: Numbered CHSH display retyped from equation to external theorem because the text names it as the CHSH inequality; its hypothesis (joint distribution) lies in the surrounding proof sentences.
Main evidence is experimental proportions in tables and bootstrap intervals; the tables themselves are not nodes, only the numerical claims stated in the text.
Experimental-design narrative (story-line pairs, Qualtrics setup) and the psychological interpretation paragraphs were left out as non-mathematical.

nodes.name: context-dependence
nodes.statement: It is commonplace to say that human behavior is \emph{context-dependent}. What is usually meant by this is that one's response to stimulus $S$ (performance in task $S$) depends on other stimuli (tasks) $S'$.
nodes.statement_short: Behavior is context-dependent when the response to stimulus $S$ depends on other stimuli $S'$.

nodes.name: pure contextuality
nodes.statement: Quantum mechanics, however, provides striking examples of another form of context-dependence, when the distribution of $R$ at a fixed $S$ does not change with $S',$ but $R$ nevertheless is not one and the same random variable at different values of $S'$. This type of context-dependence is schematically depicted in Fig.$\,$\ref{fig: contextual}, and can be called ``purely contextual.''
nodes.statement_short: Context-dependence where the distribution of $R$ does not change with $S'$ but $R$ is not the same random variable across $S'$.

nodes.name: Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradigm in the Bohm-Bell version (EPR/BB)
nodes.statement: An example of pure contextuality in quantum mechanics that is especially relevant for us (because our behavioral experiment follows its formal structure) is the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen paradigm in the Bohm-Bell version (EPR/BB, Fig.$\,$\ref{fig:EPR/B}).

nodes.name: spin variables $A_i$, $B_j$
nodes.statement: Let us denote the spins along axes $\alpha_{i}$ and $\beta_{j}$ by, respectively, $A_{i}$ and $B_{j}$.

nodes.name: EPR/BB axes force contextuality (Bell)
nodes.statement: As it turns out, the axes can be chosen so that it is impossible for the identity of $A_{i}$ not to depend on the choice of $\beta_{j}$ and for the identity of $B_{j}$ not to depend on the choice of $\alpha_{i}$.
conclusions:
it is
impossible for the identity of $A_{i}$ not to depend on the choice of $\beta_{j}$ and for the identity of $B_{j}$ not to depend on the choice of $\alpha_{i}$
nodes.statement_short: For suitable axes, $A_i$ must depend in identity on Bob's choice $\beta_j$ and $B_j$ on Alice's choice $\alpha_i$.

nodes.name: Proof of EPR/BB contextuality via CHSH violation
nodes.statement: This is established by the following reasoning. If we assume that $A_{i}$ is one and the same random variable under $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ (and analogously for $B_{j}$ under $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$), then we should have four jointly distributed random variables $A_{1},A_{2},B_{1},B_{2}$, and the observed pairs of measurements by Alice and Bob then should be derivable from this distribution as its marginals $\left(A_{1},B_{1}\right)$, $\left(A_{1},B_{2}\right)$, $\left(A_{2},B_{1}\right)$, and $\left(A_{2},B_{2}\right)$. If so, these pairwise joint distributions should satisfy the following inequality, abbreviated CHSH (Clauser, Horne, Shimony, \& Holt, 1969; Fine, 1982): \begin{equation} \max_{k,l\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\sum_{i,j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}B_{j}\right]-2\mathsf{E}\left[A_{k}B_{l}\right]\right|-2\leq0, \end{equation} where $\mathsf{E}$ is expected value. Now, the expected values in the CHSH inequality can be computed for any axes $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{1},\beta_{2}$ by using the principles of quantum mechanics, and it turns out that for certain choices of these axes these expected values violate the inequality. By reductio ad absurdum, therefore, we have to reject the initial assumption that $A_{i}$ is the same for both choices of $\beta_{j}$ and $B_{j}$ is the same for both choices of $\alpha_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Reductio: noncontextuality implies a joint distribution, hence CHSH; quantum predictions violate CHSH for some axes.

nodes.name: CHSH inequality
nodes.statement: \max_{k,l\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\sum_{i,j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}B_{j}\right]-2\mathsf{E}\left[A_{k}B_{l}\right]\right|-2\leq0,
nodes.statement_short: CHSH inequality: for jointly distributed $\pm1$ variables, the CHSH combination of pairwise expectations is at most 2.
nodes.label: eq: CHSH

nodes.name: Assume noncontextuality
nodes.statement: This is established by the following reasoning. If we assume that $A_{i}$ is one and the same random variable under $\beta_{1}$ and $\beta_{2}$ (and analogously for $B_{j}$ under $\alpha_{1}$ and $\alpha_{2}$), then we should have four jointly distributed random variables $A_{1},A_{2},B_{1},B_{2}$, and the observed pairs of measurements by Alice and Bob then should be derivable from this distribution as its marginals $\left(A_{1},B_{1}\right)$, $\left(A_{1},B_{2}\right)$, $\left(A_{2},B_{1}\right)$, and $\left(A_{2},B_{2}\right)$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume $A_i$, $B_j$ context-free; then all four are jointly distributed with the observed pairs as marginals.

nodes.name: Apply CHSH
nodes.statement: If so, these pairwise joint distributions should satisfy the following inequality, abbreviated CHSH (Clauser, Horne, Shimony, \& Holt, 1969; Fine, 1982): \begin{equation} \max_{k,l\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\sum_{i,j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}B_{j}\right]-2\mathsf{E}\left[A_{k}B_{l}\right]\right|-2\leq0, \end{equation} where $\mathsf{E}$ is expected value.
nodes.statement_short: The pairwise distributions must then satisfy the CHSH inequality.

nodes.name: Quantum violation
nodes.statement: Now, the expected values in the CHSH inequality can be computed for any axes $\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\beta_{1},\beta_{2}$ by using the principles of quantum mechanics, and it turns out that for certain choices of these axes these expected values violate the inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Quantum mechanics predicts expectations violating CHSH for some axes.

nodes.name: Reject assumption
nodes.statement: By reductio ad absurdum, therefore, we have to reject the initial assumption that $A_{i}$ is the same for both choices of $\beta_{j}$ and $B_{j}$ is the same for both choices of $\alpha_{i}$.
nodes.statement_short: Contradiction: reject context-independence of $A_i$ and $B_j$.

nodes.name: context-indexed variables $A_i^j$, $B_j^i$
nodes.statement: In other words, $A_{i}$ and $B_{j}$ measured together are in fact $A_{i}^{j}$ and $B_{j}^{i}$, so that, e.g., $A_{1}^{1}$ (Alice's measurement along axis $\alpha_{1}$ when Bob has chosen axis $\beta_{1}$) is different from $A_{1}^{2}$ (Alice's measurement along the same axis when Bob has chosen $\beta_{2}$).
nodes.statement_short: $A_i^j$ ($B_j^i$) is Alice's (Bob's) measurement along $\alpha_i$ ($\beta_j$) in the context of the other's choice $\beta_j$ ($\alpha_i$).

nodes.name: random variable
nodes.statement: A formal definition of a random variable in probability theory is that it is a measurable function mapping one probability space into another, and it is jointly distributed with any other measurable function defined on the same domain probability space.
differentia:
mapping one probability space into
another

nodes.name: marginal selectivity (no-signaling)
nodes.statement: The CHSH inequality (\ref{eq: CHSH}) and other traditional contextuality tests in quantum mechanics are derived under the assumption of ``no-signaling'' (Abramsky \& Brandenburger, 2011; Adenier \& Khrennikov, 2017) or ``marginal selectivity'' (Dzhafarov \& Kujala, 2014b), which is the condition ensuring that the context does not influence random variables directly.
nodes.origin_citation: Abramsky & Brandenburger 2011; Adenier & Khrennikov 2017; Dzhafarov & Kujala 2014b
nodes.statement_short: Marginal selectivity (no-signaling): the context does not influence the distributions of the random variables directly.

nodes.name: Violation of marginal selectivity in Aerts, Gabora & Sozzo (2013)
nodes.statement: For instance, in Aerts, Gabora, and Sozzo (2013), when choosing between Tiger and Cat (task $\alpha_{2}$), Tiger was chosen with probability 0.86 when combined with the choice between Growls and Winnies (task $\beta_{1}$), but Tiger was only chosen with probability 0.23 when combined with the choice between Snorts and Meows ($\beta_{2}$).
nodes.statement_short: Tiger chosen with probability 0.86 vs 0.23 depending on the paired sound choice, violating marginal selectivity.

nodes.name: Contextuality-by-Default (CbD)
nodes.statement: More generally, however, one can consider the possibility that the distribution of $R$ does change with $S'$, but the extent of this change is not sufficient to account for the extent of the changes in $R$'s identity, as revealed by its joint distribution with other random variables. This combined form of context-dependence has been studied in the mathematical theory called Contextuality-by-Default (CbD, Dzhafarov, Cervantes, \& Kujala, 2017; Dzhafarov \& Kujala, 2014a, 2016a, 2016b, 2017a; Dzhafarov, Kujala, \& Cervantes, 2016; Dzhafarov, Kujala, \& Larsson, 2015; Kujala, Dzhafarov, \& Larsson, 2015).
nodes.statement_short: CbD studies context-dependence where distributional change with $S'$ is insufficient to explain the change in $R$'s identity.

nodes.name: contextuality proper of the EPR/BB system (CbD)
nodes.statement: When applied to the EPR/BB system, the logic of CbD is as follows. One determines the maximal probability with which $A_{1}^{1}$ could equal $A_{1}^{2}$ if the two were jointly distributed. This probability is a measure of difference between the two distributions (the smaller the probability the larger the difference). Analogously one determines the maximal probabilities of $A_{2}^{1}=A_{2}^{2}$, $B_{1}^{1}=B_{1}^{2}$, and $B_{2}^{1}=B_{2}^{2}$. If this measure of difference between the distributions is sufficient to account for the entire difference between the random variables $A_{1}^{1}$ and $A_{1}^{2}$, $B_{1}^{1}$ and $B_{1}^{2}$, etc., then these maximal probabilities should be compatible with the observed joint distributions of $\left(A_{1}^{1},B_{1}^{1}\right)$, $\left(A_{1}^{2},B_{2}^{1}\right)$, $\left(A_{2}^{1},B_{1}^{2}\right)$, and $\left(A_{2}^{2},B_{2}^{2}\right)$. If they are, the system in noncontextual. If they are not, then $A_{1}^{1}$ and $A_{1}^{2}$, or $B_{1}^{1}$ and $B_{1}^{2}$, etc., have to be more dissimilar as random variables than they are due to the difference between their distributions. Such a system exhibits contextuality proper (``on top of'' direct influences).
nodes.statement_short: System is noncontextual iff maximal probabilities of $A_i^1=A_i^2$, $B_j^1=B_j^2$ are compatible with the observed joint distributions; else contextual.

nodes.name: CbD contextuality criterion for the EPR/BB system
nodes.statement: It is proved (Dzhafarov, Kujala, \& Larsson, 2015; Kujala \& Dzhafarov, 2016) that the EPR/BB system is noncontextual if and only if \begin{equation} \begin{array}{r} \max_{k,l\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\sum_{i,j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{j}B_{j}^{i}\right]-2\mathsf{E}\left[A_{k}^{l}B_{l}^{k}\right]\right|\\ \\ -\sum_{i\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{1}\right]-\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{2}\right]\right|\\ \\ -\sum_{j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\mathsf{E}\left[B_{j}^{1}\right]-\mathsf{E}\left[B_{j}^{2}\right]\right|-2\leq0. \end{array} \end{equation}
conclusions: the EPR/BB system is noncontextual if and only if \begin{equation} \begin{array}{r} \max_{k,l\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\sum_{i,j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{j}B_{j}^{i}\right]-2\mathsf{E}\left[A_{k}^{l}B_{l}^{k}\right]\right|\\ \\ -\sum_{i\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{1}\right]-\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{2}\right]\right|\\ \\ -\sum_{j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\mathsf{E}\left[B_{j}^{1}\right]-\mathsf{E}\left[B_{j}^{2}\right]\right|-2\leq0. \end{array}
nodes.statement_short: EPR/BB is noncontextual iff the CHSH maximum minus the marginal-difference sums is at most 2.

nodes.name: Modified CHSH inequality (CbD)
nodes.statement: \begin{array}{r} \max_{k,l\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\sum_{i,j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{j}B_{j}^{i}\right]-2\mathsf{E}\left[A_{k}^{l}B_{l}^{k}\right]\right|\\ \\ -\sum_{i\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{1}\right]-\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{2}\right]\right|\\ \\ -\sum_{j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\mathsf{E}\left[B_{j}^{1}\right]-\mathsf{E}\left[B_{j}^{2}\right]\right|-2\leq0. \end{array}
nodes.label: eq:modCHSH

nodes.name: CbD criterion generalizes CHSH
nodes.statement: The formula generalizes the CHSH inequality (\ref{eq: CHSH}), which obtains if the second and third sums in the expression are zero (no-signaling or marginal selectivity condition).

nodes.name: All behavioral context-dependence is due to direct influences
nodes.statement: This series of negative results led Dzhafarov, Zhang, and Kujala (2015) and Dzhafarov, Kujala, Cervantes, Zhang, and Jones (2016) to hypothesize that all context-dependence in behavioral and social data may be due to direct influences, with no contextuality proper.
nodes.origin_citation: Dzhafarov, Zhang & Kujala 2015; Dzhafarov, Kujala, Cervantes, Zhang & Jones 2016
conclusions:
all
context-dependence in behavioral and social data may be due to direct
influences, with no contextuality proper

nodes.name: respondents
nodes.statement: 1799 of the participants completed the experiment by answering the two questions posed to them. They will be referred to below as respondents, and their responses were used for the analysis.

nodes.name: contexts (experimental conditions)
nodes.statement: Each participant was randomly assigned to one of four conditions, referred to as contexts: see Table \ref{tab:Contexts}.

nodes.name: systems (context-content systems)
nodes.statement: We refer to these tables of proportions (or probabilities they estimate) as ``systems,'' in accordance with the terminology of ``context-content systems'' introduced in Dzhafarov \& Kujala (2016a).

nodes.name: Correct-choice system attains maximal first sum
nodes.statement: In this system, the $\max$ of the first sum in Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} equals 4 (its maximal possible value), and the presence or absence of contextuality depends only on the the relative proportions of two correct pairs of choices.

nodes.name: System of correct choices is contextual (0.452)
nodes.statement: The system is contextual on the sample level: the left-hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} equals 0.452.
conclusions: The system is contextual on the sample level
the left-hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} equals 0.452

nodes.name: Bootstrap confidence interval
nodes.statement: To evaluate how reliable this figure is, a bootstrap confidence interval (Davison \& Hinkley, 1997) was calculated by generating $n=400,000$ resamples from each of the contexts, computing the left hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} for each of them, choosing a confidence level $C,$ and finding the $\frac{1-C}{2}$ and $1-\frac{1-C}{2}$ quantiles of their distribution.
nodes.statement_short: Percentile bootstrap: resample each context, recompute the LHS of the CbD inequality, take central quantiles at level $C$.

nodes.name: Resample
nodes.statement: generating $n=400,000$ resamples from each of the contexts

nodes.name: Compute statistic
nodes.statement: computing the left hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} for each of them

nodes.name: Choose level
nodes.statement: choosing a confidence level $C,$

nodes.name: Quantiles
nodes.statement: finding the $\frac{1-C}{2}$ and $1-\frac{1-C}{2}$ quantiles of their distribution

nodes.name: Bootstrap CI for correct choices
nodes.statement: For this system, the $99.99\%$ bootstrap confidence interval for the left hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} is $[0.226,0.668]$.
conclusions: the $99.99\%$ bootstrap confidence interval for the left hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} is $[0.226,0.668]$

nodes.name: Confidence to cover zero exceeds 99.999%
nodes.statement: The confidence needed for the bootstrap interval to cover zero exceeds $99.999\%$ since none of the $400,000$ resamples produced a non-positive value.
assumptions:
none of the $400,000$ resamples produced a non-positive
value
conclusions:
The confidence needed for the bootstrap interval to cover zero exceeds
$99.999\%$

nodes.name: System of all responses is contextual (0.279)
nodes.statement: This system is contextual on the sample level: the left-hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} equals 0.279.
conclusions: This system is contextual on the sample level

the left-hand side
of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} equals 0.279

nodes.name: Bootstrap for all responses
nodes.statement: A bootstrap confidence interval was calculated by generating $n=400,000$ resamples and analyzing them in the same way as for the system of correct responses.
nodes.statement_short: Same percentile bootstrap (400,000 resamples) as for correct responses.

nodes.name: Bootstrap CI for all responses
nodes.statement: For this system, the $99.99\%$ bootstrap confidence interval for the left hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} is $[0.008,0.506]$.
conclusions: the $99.99\%$ bootstrap confidence interval for the left hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} is $[0.008,0.506]$

nodes.name: Contextuality observed in human behavior
nodes.statement: We have demonstrated that a contextual system of random variables formally analogous to the EPR/BB system in quantum mechanics can be observed in human behavior.
conclusions: a contextual system of random variables formally analogous to the EPR/BB system in quantum mechanics can be observed in human behavior

nodes.name: Marginal selectivity in EPR/BB
nodes.statement: Marginal selectivity (or no-signaling condition), in application to the EPR/BB system, means that the second and third sums in Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} are zero.

nodes.name: Equal correct-choice probabilities would give a PR box
nodes.statement: If this were the case in our experiments (e.g., if the two correct choices of the character-characteristic pairs were made with equal probability), the left hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} for the system with correct choices would have the maximal theoretically possible value, 2. This would make the system a so-called PR box (Popescu \& Rohrlich, 1994), a system forbidden by laws of both classical and quantum mechanics.
nodes.statement_short: Under marginal selectivity the correct-choice system would reach LHS value 2, a PR box forbidden classically and quantum mechanically.

nodes.name: Observed contextuality below the Tsirelson bound
nodes.statement: There is no a priori reason why a behavioral system could not violate boundaries established by quantum mechanics, but the sample level contextuality value of 0.452 obtained in our experiment for correct responses is quite moderate, well below the quantum boundary (so-called Tsirelson bound) of $2\left(\sqrt{2}-1\right)$.

nodes.name: Direct-influences-only hypothesis falsified
nodes.statement: Recall that application of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} and similar formulas to all previously reported experimental data showed no contextuality at all, leading Dzhafarov, Zhang, \& Kujala (2015) and Dzhafarov, Kujala, Cervantes, Zhang, and Jones (2016) to consider the possibility that all context-dependence in psychology is due to direct influences only. This hypothesis is now falsified.

nodes.name: Results not forced by the design
nodes.statement: Could the results reported in this paper be essentially forced by the experiment's design? It is easy to see that this is not the case.

nodes.name: Counterexample: noncontextual all-correct system
nodes.statement: For example, in Table \ref{tab:Correct-responses-1} all responses are correct but the system is noncontextual, with the left-hand side of Inequality \ref{eq:modCHSH} equal to -0.004. No superficial inspection of this system would reveal a qualitative difference from the one in Table \ref{tab:Correct-responses}.
nodes.statement_short: A hypothetical all-correct system (Table 4) is noncontextual (LHS $-0.004$), so the design does not force contextuality.

nodes.name: Design maximizes the first term
nodes.statement: The experimental design we use (considering only correct responses) makes the value \begin{equation} \max_{k,l\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\sum_{i,j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{j}B_{j}^{i}\right]-2\mathsf{E}\left[A_{k}^{l}B_{l}^{k}\right]\right| \end{equation} equal to 4, its maximal possible value.
conclusions: equal to 4, its maximal possible value

nodes.name: CHSH maximum term
nodes.statement: \max_{k,l\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\sum_{i,j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{j}B_{j}^{i}\right]-2\mathsf{E}\left[A_{k}^{l}B_{l}^{k}\right]\right|
nodes.label: eq: first

nodes.name: Contextuality determined by the marginal-difference sum
nodes.statement: The system's (non)contextuality therefore is determined entirely by the value of \begin{equation} \sum_{i\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{1}\right]-\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{2}\right]\right|+\sum_{j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\mathsf{E}\left[B_{j}^{1}\right]-\mathsf{E}\left[B_{j}^{2}\right]\right|. \end{equation} The system is contextual if and only if this expression's value is less than 2.
conclusions:
The system is contextual if and only if this expression's value is
less than 2
equivalent_conditions:
this expression's value is
less than 2
nodes.statement_short: With the first term equal to 4, the system is contextual iff the sum of marginal expectation differences is below 2.

nodes.name: Sum of marginal expectation differences
nodes.statement: \sum_{i\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{1}\right]-\mathsf{E}\left[A_{i}^{2}\right]\right|+\sum_{j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} }\left|\mathsf{E}\left[B_{j}^{1}\right]-\mathsf{E}\left[B_{j}^{2}\right]\right|.
nodes.label: eq: the sum

nodes.name: marginal expectations $a,b,c,d$
nodes.statement: In the system of correct responses \begin{equation} \begin{array}{c} a=\mathsf{E}\left[A_{1}^{1}\right]=\mathsf{E}\left[B_{1}^{1}\right],\\ b=\mathsf{E}\left[A_{1}^{2}\right]=\mathsf{E}\left[B_{2}^{1}\right],\\ c=\mathsf{E}\left[A_{2}^{1}\right]=\mathsf{E}\left[B_{1}^{2}\right],\\ d=\mathsf{E}\left[A_{2}^{2}\right]=-\mathsf{E}\left[B_{2}^{2}\right]. \end{array} \end{equation} Each of the four values $a,b,c,d$ ranges between $-1$ and $1$.

nodes.name: Marginal expectations in the correct-response system
nodes.statement: \begin{array}{c} a=\mathsf{E}\left[A_{1}^{1}\right]=\mathsf{E}\left[B_{1}^{1}\right],\\ b=\mathsf{E}\left[A_{1}^{2}\right]=\mathsf{E}\left[B_{2}^{1}\right],\\ c=\mathsf{E}\left[A_{2}^{1}\right]=\mathsf{E}\left[B_{1}^{2}\right],\\ d=\mathsf{E}\left[A_{2}^{2}\right]=-\mathsf{E}\left[B_{2}^{2}\right]. \end{array}

nodes.name: Probability that a random correct-response system is noncontextual
nodes.statement: It is reasonable now to ask how probable it is that these four values chosen ``randomly and independently'' (meaning that the quadruple of the expected values is uniformly distributed within the 4-dimensional cube) would yield (\ref{eq: the sum}) equal to or exceeding 2.
nodes.statement_short: Probability that uniform random $(a,b,c,d)\in[-1,1]^4$ gives marginal-difference sum $\ge 2$.

nodes.name: Noncontextuality probability about 0.6667
nodes.statement: The answer is easily obtained by Monte Carlo simulation, and the probability in question, i.e., the probability that a randomly created system is noncontextual, turns out to be about 0.6667.
conclusions:
the probability that a randomly created system
is noncontextual, turns out to be about 0.6667

nodes.name: direct influences (CbD)
nodes.statement: Although the initial intuition of direct influences involves conventional schemes with forces and energy transfer, in the mathematical theory direct influences are \emph{defined} by the differences between the distributions of random variables measuring (responding to) the same property in different contexts.
nodes.statement_short: In CbD, direct influences are the differences between distributions of variables measuring the same property in different contexts.

nodes.name: EPR/BB is a cyclic system of rank 4
nodes.statement: In the terminology of CbD, the EPR/BB system is a cyclic system of rank 4 (Dzhafarov, Kujala, \& Larsson, 2015; Kujala, Dzhafarov, \& Larsson, 2015).
nodes.origin_citation: Dzhafarov, Kujala & Larsson 2015; Kujala, Dzhafarov & Larsson 2015

nodes.name: Design maximizing contextuality in EPR/BB experiments
nodes.statement: This system involves eight binary random variables, $A_{j}^{i}$, $B_{i}^{j}$ ($i,j\in\left\{ 1,2\right\} $), and the design maximizing the chances of this system exhibiting contextuality (``on top of'' direct influences) is as follows. Label the values of all the random variables $+1$ and $-1$ and create a ``story line'' in which +1 of $A_{j}^{i}$ and +1 of $B_{i}^{j}$ are associated with a very high probability in three out of four pairs $\left(A_{j}^{i},B_{i}^{j}\right)$, and with a very low probability in the fourth pair (or vice versa).
nodes.statement_short: Code all variables $\pm1$ and build a story line where +1s co-occur with high probability in three contexts and low in the fourth.

nodes.name: Label values
nodes.statement: Label the values of all the random variables $+1$ and $-1$

nodes.name: Create story line
nodes.statement: create a ``story line'' in which +1 of $A_{j}^{i}$ and +1 of $B_{i}^{j}$ are associated with a very high probability in three out of four pairs $\left(A_{j}^{i},B_{i}^{j}\right)$, and with a very low probability in the fourth pair (or vice versa)

nodes.name: Extension to other cyclic systems
nodes.statement: For other cyclic systems (say, of ranks 3 or 5) the criteria of contextuality are similar to (\ref{eq:modCHSH}), and the design can be constructed similarly.

nodes.name: contextuality analysis (CbD)
nodes.statement: Contextuality analysis consists in finding out whether a joint distribution can be \emph{imposed} on these eight random variables, subject to certain constraints (maximality of the probabilities of $A_{1}^{1}=A_{1}^{2}$, $B_{1}^{1}=B_{1}^{2}$, etc.).
